* * * It comes as no surprise^. . .that “the action of the federal 
government in recogmzing or failing to recognize a tribe has 
traditionally been held to be a political one not subject to judicial 
review.”
But this conclusion assumes that the executive branch has not 
sought to canalize the discretion of its subordinate officials by means 
of regulations that require them to base recognition of Indian tribes 
on the kinds of determination, legal or factual, that courts routinely 
make. By proTrigating such regulations [as Interior had done in 
1978] the executive brings the tribal recognition process within the 
scope of the Administrative Procedure Act. And the Act has been 
interpreted (1) to require agencies, on pain of being found to have 
acted arbitrarily and capriciously, to comply with their own 
regulations * * * and (2) to make comphance with the regulations 
judicially reviewable, provided there is law to apply to determine 
comphance. * * *
In addressing this last qualification Judge Posner went on to observe:
[A]s the “law to apply” provision of the APA makes clear, the fact 
that a regulation has been promulgated doesn’t automatically make 
comphance with the regulation a justiciable issue. It depends on what 
the regulation says; it may not set forth sufficiently law-like criteria 
to provide guideposts for a reasoned judicial decision.
Judge Posner then turned to the text of the Interior regulations, which set 
forth seven criteria that a tribe must satisfy to be ehgible for recognition, 
including historical continuity, occupancy of a specific area, maintenance ot 
tribal authority over community members, adherence to a written gover^g 
document, and documentation of tribal membership. Judge Posner found tha 
these criteria posed factual and legal questions of “the sort * * * that coiirts are 
equipped to answer.” He then proceeded to evaluate the Interior Departmen s 
explanation for its refusal to recognize the tribe and, save for an error he toun 
harmless, concluded that its decision should be upheld.
3. REVIEW OF AGENCY INACTION
The traditional law of judicial review of administrative action is 
largely the product of a concern to protect private interests from unlawiui 
assertions of governmental authority. In recent decades, however, muc 
attention has been given to the failure of administrative agencies o en orce 
existing standards or to develop standards adequate to protect the pub c 
interest. Judicial review is frequently sought not to restoin, u o 
stimulate, administrative action. See generally Mernck: B. Garland, 
Deregulation and Judicial Review, 98 HARV. L. REV. 505 (1985); Cass R 
Sunstein, Deregulation and the Hard-Look Doctrine, 1983 SUP.
177.
